name: Pre-Marxist communism
summary: Pre-Marxist communism covers the early demands for common ownership of land and goods, from Winstanley's Diggers and Morelly to Babeuf's Conspiracy of the Equals and Cabet's Icarians. It holds that private property is the root of inequality and misery and seeks a community of goods with real, not merely legal, equality. Most strands combine this with republican or Christian moral appeals and differ on whether to use insurrection or model communities.
scope: The seventeenth to mid-nineteenth century egalitarian-communist current: Gerrard Winstanley and the Diggers, Morelly, Babeuf and the Manifesto of the Equals, and Cabet and the Icarians (with Dezamy and Leroux in the background). It excludes Marxism and later communist movements, and the earlier religious and ancient strands (Plato, Mazdak, Muntzer) except where they overlap; Babouvists were secular and insurrectionary while Winstanley and Cabet were Christian and mostly pacific, so contested answers are marked low.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wages themselves are the target, since the Equals planned to end money and collectivize production; a higher legal wage would be a reform of the system they reject, though not opposed as harm.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Winstanley's Platform is explicitly a government of the earth without buying and selling, with storehouses as common stock, so markets are rejected outright.

public-ownership.rationale: The Equals' draft decree had the national community's goods exploited collectively, so major industries would be held in common by the whole community.

unions-good.rationale: Pre-industrial and early industrial thinkers rarely addressed trade unions; Babeuf's circle and Cabet's followers favoured worker cooperatives over wage bargaining, so no firm stance.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals declares the land belongs to no one and its fruits to all, and seeks abolition of private property.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Equals denounced a system where most toil for a tiny minority and demanded a common provision of needs, so cutting support for the poor opposes their core aims.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Cabet's Icaria closely supervised social life, but no pre-Marxist source addresses terrorism surveillance; adherents are split between authoritarian and libertarian strands.

strong-leader.rationale: The Equals sought a Republic of Equals with no rulers and ruled distinction, though Babeuf's conspiracy relied on a small directing group; a strong bypassing leader is not endorsed.

state-harmful.rationale: They wanted a democratic Republic of Equals that ends the division of rulers and ruled, but not abolition of public authority; Winstanley kept officers and laws, so the state as such is not rejected.

empower-police-military.rationale: Winstanley kept officers to enforce laws but sought a peaceful commonwealth with no kings and no standing coercive state; more power for police and army is not a goal.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Diggers rejected sexual licence associated with the Ranters and Cabet's rules were strict; sex work as a market transaction conflicts with no-money communities.

decide-locally.rationale: Icarian and Digger communities governed themselves by local meetings, but the Equals planned a national republic, so the preference is mixed.

traditional-family.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet kept the nuclear family as the one independent unit, while Plato and Morelly-type strands abolished it; the strands split on this.

more-religion-public.rationale: Strands diverge sharply: Winstanley, Cabet and Muntzer drew on scripture and Acts 4:32, while Babeuf's Equals and Morelly were deist or secular.

gradual-change.rationale: The Manifesto demands real equality now, calls legal equality a sterile fiction and anticipates a final greater revolution, so cautious respect for existing institutions is rejected.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: No international bodies existed in this period; universalist strands might welcome them but none planned them.

free-trade.rationale: Winstanley's commonwealth abolishes buying and selling and the Equals and Cabet abolished money, so trade as a general benefit is rejected in principle.

nation-first.rationale: Christian and Enlightenment universalism pervades these strands, so putting national interest ahead of cooperation is not their stance, though communities were locally focused.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The Babouvists were absorbed in domestic revolution; no pre-Marxist source discusses foreign intervention.

limit-growth.rationale: Environmental limits were not a concern, though Winstanley's ecological outlook and Rousseau's critique of luxury hint at sympathy for sufficiency; split.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The Manifesto says let all the arts perish if need be for equality, while Cabet's Icaria prized industry; adherents split on technology's role.

revolution-justified.rationale: Split: Babeuf preached insurrection and planned a rising in 1796, while Cabet and Winstanley preferred peaceful founding of communities.

experts-over-public.rationale: The Equals wanted equality in education and no distinction between rulers and ruled, though Plato's guardians and Saint-Simon-like strands favoured experts; the typical communist leans populist.

central-planning.rationale: Cabet's Icaria has an elected body controlling all economic activity and the Equals' decree exploited goods collectively, implying a planned economy by the community.

socialized-markets.rationale: Their ideal abolished buying and selling altogether, so markets even among common owners are not their goal, though such markets would be a lesser evil.

land-value-tax.rationale: They wanted land to belong to no one and its fruits to all, so taxing land value to leave private landholding intact falls short of their aim.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The Equals' draft decree abolished inheritance, with property passing to the national community at death, so heavy taxes on large inheritances are a mild form of their position.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade policy was not their concern since they aimed at a moneyless community economy.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Under Cabet's elected body directing the economy, investment would be directed by the community, though they did not frame it as strategic industrial policy.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Manifesto contrasts its aim with the old agrarian law of dividing land, which it dismisses, wanting common ownership instead of small holdings.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The Equals' draft decree said the republic will no longer make money and Winstanley's Platform abolishes buying and selling; wage labour ends with common storehouses.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: They would end money altogether rather than hand it to the market, so abolishing central banks to free money for markets is not their aim even though the abolition coincides.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Equals sought to abolish class distinctions, not to organise employers and workers into bargaining bodies that preserve them.

one-party-rule.rationale: Babeuf's conspirators were a secret directing society, but their goal was a republic on the 1793 constitution; later Buonarroti-style views split on a party guide.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Winstanley opposes kingly rule, likening it to the government of scribes and Pharisees, and the Equals demanded a republic where rulers and ruled are not divided.

democracy-best.rationale: The Equals demanded the democratic 1793 constitution and Cabet's Icaria and Nauvoo used elected bodies, but the Manifesto subordinates formal politics to real equality.

direct-votes.rationale: The Equals demanded the 1793 constitution, which provided for ratification of laws by the people, and Nauvoo members met weekly to discuss community affairs.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Manifesto insists all share the same faculties and needs and wants no distinctions other than age and sex, rejecting a naturally superior ruling class.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Babouvists planned insurrection and Muntzer waged war, so violence is not ruled out, though Winstanley and Cabet's colonists renounced it as a method.

war-builds-character.rationale: These strands condemned wars and the crimes of the propertied; Rousseau blamed property for wars and murders, so war as ennobling is not endorsed.

separate-church-state.rationale: Strands split: Babeuf's circle and Jansenist-influenced radicals tended toward secular republic while Winstanley and Cabet wanted a Christian-inspired commonwealth.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Winstanley grounded his Platform in Scripture and Cabet claimed Jesus preached communism, but the Equals and Morelly rested on reason and nature; split.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Winstanley's officers and magistrates are public and common, and the Equals sought no private power over others, so privatized courts and defence contradict the aim.

military-superiority.rationale: None of these strands aimed at rivalry among states; they were domestic or utopian projects.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Universal brotherhood of mankind is the premise of Equals, Cabet and Christian communism, so ethnic definition of the nation is not endorsed.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The idea was later Marxist; Engels read Muntzer and the Levellers as class struggles, but the Equals framed it as the many against the few without a general theory.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Manifesto rejects legal equality as a sterile fiction and demands real equality in education, food and goods, we want real equality or death.

civilizational-union.rationale: Their universalism points to humanity as a whole, not unions of civilizations.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Manifesto and Winstanley's commonwealth condemn the minority living on the sweat of the many and place the common good above private gain.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Winstanley requires labour of all and punishes idleness, and Cabet's Icarian rules demanded conduct and submission to the community, so duty to the commons is prominent.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Winstanley's views on creation and the earth were ecological, but intrinsic value of nature in the modern sense is an inference; others did not address it.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Manifesto's willingness to let the arts perish expresses disdain for refined society, but these strands are not anti-industrial; Cabet's Icaria embraced industry.

restore-past-order.rationale: The Manifesto looks forward to a final greater revolution, though Winstanley and Cabet appealed to the primitive Christian community and Seneca's golden age, so a backward-looking strand exists.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The Equals demanded real equality as a principle whose truth does not depend on outcomes, and they tied their cause firmly to doctrine.

direct-action.rationale: Nulled: the statement now asks whether direct action should replace electoral politics (reworded 2026-11-10, Codex review). This answer rested on direct action used alongside elections or on a mixed record, which does not support agreeing that it should replace them; its sources need re-reading against the new text.

reviewHistory.rationale: The Diggers acted by planting common land without waiting for Parliament and the Babouvists planned insurrection, but Cabet and others petitioned and founded colonies.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled: the statement now asks whether direct action should replace electoral politics (reworded 2026-11-10, Codex review). This answer rested on direct action used alongside elections or on a mixed record, which does not support agreeing that it should replace them; its sources need re-reading against the new text.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Seneca and others idealised a primitive golden age of common goods, but none argued for a return to hunting and gathering as the program.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The Manifesto wants everyone to share one education and food and no distinction beyond age and sex, but it did not call for abolishing specialised work; later Marxists did.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The Manifesto bases one education and one standard of food on common faculties and needs and Winstanley's storehouses are a common stock for each family.

production-for-use.rationale: Winstanley's households fill storehouses as common stock without buying and selling, so goods are produced for the commonwealth's needs rather than for profit.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Manifesto complains the great majority work and sweat for the smallest of minorities and Leroux argued private ownership of the means of production enables exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Not a pre-Marxist term; the Babouvists planned a transitional revolutionary authority, but there is no doctrine of working-class rule over the former rulers.

collective-farming.rationale: Winstanley's families plant and harvest by common assistance and the Equals sought collective exploitation of land, though Winstanley kept separate households.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Rousseau blamed private property for crimes and wars, but no pre-Marxist strand elaborated capitalism leading to imperial war.

harm-principle.rationale: Cabet's Icaria supervised social life and Winstanley punished offences sharply, so the limited-state principle is not theirs, but they did not argue against it.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Their focus was the community of goods and a Republic of Equals, so rights belonging only to individuals is not their frame.

conscription.rationale: The Babouvists sought the 1793 republic, whose levee en masse mobilised citizens, but Winstanley's pacific commonwealth would not; split.

exit-over-voice.rationale: They place decisive power in equal democratic citizenship and common ownership, so the freedom to exit is not seen as the check on rulers.

state-as-business.rationale: The Manifesto condemns commerce-driven society and seeks community of goods, so treating citizens as customers contradicts it.

positive-liberty.rationale: Winstanley held that true freedom lies where a man receives his nourishment, in the use of the earth, which is freedom requiring material means.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The Manifesto bases equality on the shared faculties and needs of all, which excludes inherited ability gaps between groups.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Equals proclaimed a final greater revolution but not a rebirth from decadence of a nation.

territorial-expansion.rationale: These movements opposed conquest and the rule of the propertied, and the Equals' appeal was universal.

universal-morality.rationale: Rousseau, Morelly's Code of Nature and Christian communists grounded equality in nature or divine law, and the Manifesto appeals to the shared faculties of all.

single-common-good.rationale: The Manifesto speaks of the common good or the community of goods and Winstanley seeks a single commonwealth, so politics aims at one common good rather than balancing interests.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: No strand dealt with Zionism, which arose after them; the Equals and Cabet's universal framework gives no basis for a national-state claim either way.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: None of these movements treated diasporas; Cabet's emigrants founded new colonies rather than claiming an ancestral homeland.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Equals wanted one education for all, which excludes parents choosing among schools with vouchers.

economic-freedom.rationale: They held that freedom depends on equal access to the earth, not on a market economy, so political freedom does not require market economic freedom in their sense.

rule-by-example.rationale: Cabet's and Winstanley's colonies relied on exemplary communities and virtue, but Cabet also imposed forty-eight rules of conduct, so law was not absent.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The Equals and Morelly appealed to reason and nature while Winstanley, Cabet and Muntzer rested on faith; the strands split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The Manifesto's equality is universal, with no distinction apart from age and sex, so reserving benefits to citizens is not their stance.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Winstanley's Platform says there shall be no idle person or beggar and punishes those living idle on others' labour, so able people must work.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Equals attacked the rich minority living off the many and aimed to end division between rich and poor, though Cabet hoped to win all classes by persuasion.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The Manifesto says let all the arts perish if need be, but it is a rhetorical priority of equality; the directors of the revolt disputed the line.

dominated-front.rationale: Resistance to leading Western powers is a twentieth-century anti-colonial theme, absent from these domestically focused early communists.

workers-nation.rationale: These strands were universalist in orientation rather than nationally organised.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet kept conventional households and Nauvoo women could speak but not vote, while Plato and the Equals leaned to equal treatment; the strands split.

ban-interest.rationale: Winstanley's Platform and the Equals' moneyless plans leave no place for lending at interest, though it was not singled out for legal ban.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Manifesto's equality of faculties and needs for all is flatly against racial classification and separation.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The Manifesto and Winstanley describe government by a rich minority over the many, but the formal theory of the state as a ruling-class tool is Marxist.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy theories of a replacement plot do not fit communist strands whose premise is the equality of all human beings.

national-mission.rationale: The Equals expected a revolution greater than the French one that would spread equality, but not a national mission to export government form.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Manifesto condemns governments of the 1791 and 1795 charters as tightening chains and Winstanley says officers became covetous and proud, so ruling elites are corrupt and distant.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Equality of faculties and needs among all people rules out discouraging births on hereditary grounds.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The executed Babouvists were victims of state repression, so accountability for abuses would be welcome, but no program states it.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Cabet's Icaria and Winstanley's commonwealth give public authorities control of economic life, not a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Equality of all persons in the Manifesto contradicts racial hierarchies.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Manifesto demands real equality, wants no distinctions apart from age and sex and ends divisions of rich and poor, masters and servants.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A later Marxist-Leninist debate; the Babouvists planned a republic in France and Cabet colonies were local, with a general revolution anticipated as greater.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Cabet's colonists settled in Texas and Illinois without addressing displacement.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Winstanley's religion was dissenting and persecuted while the Equals were secular, so legal restriction on conversion is not typical.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Strands split: Cabet's Icaria was Christian-inspired with no denominational services in Nauvoo, Winstanley wanted children trained in godly respect, and the Equals were secular.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Equals demanded the 1793 constitution of popular sovereignty and Rousseau argued popular sovereignty, so authority rests on consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Without buying and selling there is no export strategy; a mercantilist aim is not theirs.

population-transfer.rationale: The Manifesto's equality of all and rejection of distinction contradicts expelling a minority.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Babouvists accepted insurrection and Muntzer war, so initiating force is not always wrong, though Winstanley and Cabet's colonists were pacific.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Manifesto condemns a society where the many sweat for the few and the Platform abolishes buying and selling for a commonwealth of mutual assistance.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The Manifesto objects to the division between masters and servants and rulers and ruled, a complaint about domination by the powerful.

separated-powers.rationale: The Equals favoured the 1793 constitution, which concentrated power in an assembly, while Winstanley's Platform gave officers separate functions; split.

vanguard-party.rationale: The Babouvist conspiracy was a small directing society that Marx called the first active communist party, but whether the people need such a body was not argued as doctrine.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Manifesto condemns the minority that controls what belongs to twenty million and Acts 4:32 communism inspired the Diggers' care for the poor.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: No stance was documented, but their sympathy with workers against employers excludes legal restriction.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Rousseau, Leroux and the Equals located the causes of suffering in property and social institutions.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Manifesto grounds its program on the shared faculties and needs of all people, so difference among groups is not a threat to common life.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Jacobin precedent in the Terror admired by some, while the Equals demanded the 1793 constitution's protections; split.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The Babouvists drew on the Jacobin Maximum and the Terror's price fixing for the sans-culottes, and the Manifesto aimed at secure food for all.

party-controls-media.rationale: Babeuf's journal was clandestine and the Equals fought censorship, so government control of media is not part of the platform.

party-commands-army.rationale: Babeuf's conspirators planned to place agents in the army, but ruling-party command of the army is a later doctrine.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The conspiracy was a clandestine organisation with directing members, but binding party discipline as a principle is a later doctrine.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Winstanley opposed kingly rule and the Equals demanded a republic, so a head commanding the armed forces is against them.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Waldensians, Dulcinians and Diggers opposed church hierarchy and Dolcino sought its dissolution.

clerical-rule.rationale: The strands criticised the clergy, and Mazdak and Dolcino attacked priestly hierarchy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A later Zimmerwald doctrine; the Equals fought their own government but this was not framed for war.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Plato would censor art and Cabet's Nauvoo imposed conduct rules, while the Equals proposed to let arts perish if needed; the strands are split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The sources discuss who rules but not term limits; the 1793 constitution's short terms hint at rotation but are not decisive.

recall-officials.rationale: The Jacobin tradition and the 1793 constitution favoured popular control, and the Equals wanted rulers answerable, but recall itself was not a specific demand.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy is not treated in the Manifesto of the Equals or by Winstanley or Cabet.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Winstanley and the Equals abolished private landholding so no one rents from owners, though the answer is that housing is common not individually owned, matching only half.

people-in-arms.rationale: The Jacobin and Babouvist tradition favoured the armed people over professional troops for the republic, but it was not a distinct plank.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Diggers farmed common land and Winstanley held true freedom lies in the use of the earth, and Seneca idealised an agrarian golden age.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Nationally divided borders drawn by outsiders are not a theme in these sources.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Winstanley attacked the clergy and learned lawyers but also wanted children educated; the Equals wanted universal education.

death-penalty.rationale: Winstanley's Platform proposes sharp punishment, in the Law of Freedom including capital offences for some crimes, but the opened page did not state it; Babouvist Jacobinism accepted terror; split.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Winstanley wanted all children educated but no content on sex education.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Cabet's rules and Winstanley's moral order favoured restraint, but nothing is documented on pornography.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The Equals' universalism does not tie citizenship to ancestry.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Cabet's Icaria had close supervision of social life, so non-conformity was not encouraged.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The question had no analogue, though they would abolish debt along with money.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Manifesto calls legal equality a beautiful and sterile fiction and demands that real equality extend into homes and property, so formal independence without economic change is empty.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Equals demanded the Year 1 constitution adopted by the Convention, so elected assembly constitution-making is acceptable.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Growth was not their goal and the Equals asserted equality, not output.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The 1793 constitution had an executive council chosen by the legislature, so direct election was not their form.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The Equals would end money and have the republic no longer mint it, so independent technocratic management of it is foreign.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial bargains between states are absent from these domestically oriented movements.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Equals and Winstanley hold that the earth and its fruits belong to all, which goes beyond the statement: they reject private property rather than accepting it on condition.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance doctrine such as an attack on one being an attack on all is not treated by any source.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Not clearly addressed; Jacobin-influenced radicals might, Christian communists rarely.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Winstanley opposes kingly rule and the Equals wanted a republic, which leaves no place for a sacred ruler; neither discusses divine descent.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The Manifesto's radical equality opposes regressive-leaning flat taxes, but taxation was not its instrument.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Manifesto rests equality on common faculties and the call for one education for all, and Rousseau and Owen-like thinkers held circumstances shape people.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Winstanley's Platform says kings' old laws cannot govern a free commonwealth and rulers under it are bound to publicly set laws.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Manifesto sought a Republic of Equals without orders of few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: The Manifesto ends divisions of rulers and ruled, though Cabet in 1855 sought presidency for life; the typical position opposes leader cults.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Manifesto asks that land belong to no one and its fruits to all, which is common ownership rather than distribution to farmers; the agrarian-law style division it distinguished itself from, so taking estates is supported but not giving them to individuals.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return is a modern conflict question absent from these sources.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Universal human equality as the basis of the program excludes ethnic territorial claims.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Diggers were dissenters persecuted for their beliefs, and Winstanley's faith was personal, so punishing leaving a religion is opposed.

women-must-cover.rationale: The Diggers rejected licence but nothing documents a dress law; the Equals had none.

common-currency.rationale: They wanted to end money, not unify currencies.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority self-government within a state is a later central-European question, not found in these sources.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Cabet himself led emigrants to America, while the Equals fought at home.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Marxist theory; Engels read earlier movements this way, but earlier thinkers like Winstanley and the Equals explained history by ideas and moral claims as well as property.

ban-cartels.rationale: The Equals want abolition of private concentrations of economic power rather than competition rules between owners.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The 1793 constitution's popular sovereignty emphasised majority will, but protection of rights against majority was also valued.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Diggers and Icarian colonies aimed at self-supporting communities, but not national autarky.

moral-incentives.rationale: Cabet's Icaria and Nauvoo relied on a sense of duty and communal feeling rather than money incentives, and Winstanley's commonwealth replaces trade with common labour.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The Babouvist conspiracy planned a rising by a small directing group and a network of agents, which Blanqui later developed; Cabet and Winstanley rejected it.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Manifesto wants to end divisions of rulers and ruled, rich and poor, and its draft decree abolished inheritance and privilege.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Manifesto ends divisions of rulers and ruled, so permanent or temporary rule of societies by those deemed advanced contradicts it.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Equals wanted one education for all but did not specify national loyalty content; Jacobin patriotism was strong, so split.

public-money-creation.rationale: The Equals' decree that the republic will no longer make money, along with community of goods, replaces private bank creation with a public rule, but sees abolition rather than public issue.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The Manifesto foresees a final greater revolution to overthrow new tyrants, which supposes no adaptation.

delink-world-market.rationale: Dependency theory is twentieth century, and the early communists wrote about local common stores and no global trade.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Equals demand real equality extending into the household and no distinctions, the opposite of a private right to discriminate.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Equals championed the constitution of 1793 with its declaration of rights, but this was in the context of a democratic assembly.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Equals rejected kings and took the 1793 republican constitution as their model, though they planned an insurrectionary authority before any election.

minority-veto.rationale: The Equals sought a republic with majority rule on the 1793 constitution and Cabet's Nauvoo decided by meetings, not by individual vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Babeuf preached revolt against a government that had abandoned the 1793 constitution, and the Diggers contested lawless landlords.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The 1793 constitution made the legislature central, but the Equals saw the Convention and later assemblies as having failed them.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal welfare does not appear in the Manifesto, Winstanley's Platform or Cabet's works, though Winstanley's reverence for creation hints at sympathy.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Manifesto demands abolition of rich and poor rather than a charitable duty of the privileged.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Diggers and Icarians withdrew to build colonies but in order to remake society, and the Babouvists were political activists.

native-born-offices.rationale: The Equals' universalism does not reserve offices by birth, though they did not address it.

party-own-road.rationale: Relations among national communist parties arise only after the Internationals; the Equals were a single French conspiracy.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism does not appear in the Equals, Digger or Icarian writings.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Descendants of pre-colonial peoples ruling settlers is a modern question that these sources do not treat.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument controversies are modern; the sources discuss neither statues nor commemoration of controversial figures.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The Babouvists planned to win soldiers but sought a civil republic, not army guardianship.

filial-duty.rationale: Winstanley's Platform trains children to respect parents and elders.

office-by-exam.rationale: Plato's guardians were selected by training, but others used election; split.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Winstanley's Platform has each person keep their own spouse, but the Equals took no position and Cabet kept the family.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.

reviewHistory.rationale: The popular sovereignty of the Equals' 1793 constitution favoured accountability to the people, but no explicit instruction of delegates.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The Equals wanted a common stock for all needs, so private individual accounts contradict them.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The Manifesto says the land belongs to no one and its fruits belong to all, and Winstanley's commons were used by those who work them.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The Equals deny private landholding altogether, so ownership by foreigners is moot.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Legal doctrine on disparate impact is modern and absent from these sources, which demand equality in outcomes generally.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Rousseau and the Equals denounced luxury and the Manifesto would let the arts perish for equality, and Cabet's Nauvoo banned tobacco and liquor.

job-guarantee.rationale: Winstanley's Platform has no idle persons or beggars and a common storehouse for each family, so everyone is set to work.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Babouvists rejected the constitutions of 1791 and 1795 as unjust but demanded obedience to the 1793 one; split.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Equals blamed property and the rich minority as a class, not a secret ethnic or religious conspiracy.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet maintained family and marriage, while only some strands such as Plato abolished the family for rulers; legal marriage is not typically opposed.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Reformers opposed secrecy of old regime, but the Babouvists themselves were clandestine; weak inference.

local-production.rationale: Winstanley's families fill local storehouses and Diggers and Icarians built small self-supplying communes.

religious-nation.rationale: The Equals' universal outlook disfavours religion-defined nation, though Christian communists spoke of Christian brotherhood.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The Equals attacked ritual deference of subjects to rulers and masters.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Community of goods pools wealth for all, which is opposed to local retention by richer regions.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Equal common provision is their aim, rather than a mix of private providers.

religion-illusion.rationale: Winstanley, Cabet and Muntzer drew communism from scripture, so religion as mere illusion is not typical, though Babouvists were secular.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Manifesto wants no distinctions except age and sex, so women's equality as an economic question was not framed.

socialized-care.rationale: Cabet kept the nuclear family as an independent unit while Plato abolished it for guardians; split.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism is not found in the Equals, Winstanley or Cabet.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Split: Cabet's Icarians and Winstanley's Diggers founded small common-property colonies, while the Babouvists planned a national community run through the state.

majority-settlement.rationale: Equality for all means no settlement scheme favouring one group.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The Manifesto says the land belongs to no one, which denies claims on historical grounds.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Manifesto condemns the many working for the few, which extends against colonial extraction.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Rebellion against rulers for not governing by religious law is not a position these sources take, though Winstanley invoked Scripture against kings.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Nauvoo members met weekly to discuss community affairs under universal male suffrage, and Cabet's elected body ran Icaria, so common decisions are made directly.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectionality is modern; the sources treat class and a few distinctions without a theory of overlap.

assisted-dying.rationale: Medical ethics of this kind is absent from these sources.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: They take a firm egalitarian side against the rich minority, so the claim that the best of each side should be combined is rejected.

alienated-labor.rationale: The Manifesto complains the many work and sweat for the few and Leroux described the proletariat as a revival of slavery, but alienation as a theory is Marx's.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet rooted authority in God and Christ, but the Equals and Rousseau in the people; split.

social-market-economy.rationale: They reject markets entirely: buying and selling abolished in Winstanley's Platform and money abolished by the Equals.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Babeuf's plot depended on armed force, and Winstanley sought peace; split.

rich-first.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals demands real equality at once and treats any rich minority as the evil to end; it does not discuss staged growth.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hereditary privilege is abolished in the Equals' decree and Winstanley opposed kingly rule.

property-franchise.rationale: The Equals demanded the 1793 constitution of universal suffrage against the property-based constitutions of 1791 and 1795 that they condemned.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The Manifesto calls legal equality a sterile fiction without real equality, the same logic as formal freedom of press being worthless where the rich own the means.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Winstanley's Platform sets out a codified body of laws applied by officers to replace the kings' old laws.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a minority contradicts the universal equality of the Manifesto.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Nauvoo's meetings and the direct tradition of the 1793 constitution support citizen deliberation, but random selection was not used.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Cabet reinterpreted Christianity as essentially communist in Le vrai christianisme, and Winstanley read Scripture anew, though Babouvists were secular.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Manifesto says fewer than a million control what belongs to twenty million and the Equals call it incompatible with real equality; Winstanley says freedom lies in the use of earth.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Winstanley, Cabet and Muntzer were religious, and Babouvists pursued no atheist campaign, so state promotion of atheism is opposed.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Winstanley's Platform keeps officers and sharp punishment of offenders, so police and prisons are not abolished.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Consociational power-sharing is a modern device; none of these movements wrote about it.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Contested: Winstanley's Christian strand and Cabet's Icarians differed from the secular Babouvists, and none made this a stated demand.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The strands split: Winstanley's Law of Freedom kept fatherly rule while the Equals and Icarians stressed equality, so no single answer is documented.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals and Winstanley both condemn living off others' labour and want a commonwealth where all work and none buys, sells or lives on property.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Babouvists planned armed insurrection, while Winstanley and Cabet were mostly pacific without an absolute ban; contested, so a mild no.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Split: Winstanley framed politics as a Christian struggle between Christ and kingly power, while the Babouvists were secular.

culture-before-state.rationale: Split: Cabet and Winstanley relied on persuasion and example first, while the Babouvists sought to seize the state by insurrection.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The Equals demanded real equality and popular sovereignty under the 1793 constitution, and Winstanley rejected rule by kings and landlords; common ownership was meant to serve the people, not a ruling elite.

municipal-property.rationale: Property was to be owned by the national community (the Equals' national community of goods) or by the single Icarian commonwealth, not by individual towns.

person-over-state.rationale: Equality of persons is central in the Manifesto, though the Equals and Cabet subordinated individual interest to the common good, so adherents are only partly aligned.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet grounded communism in Christian morality, while Babouvists were secular and materialist, so the answer is contested.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals appeals to equality of all human beings and the common good of the people, not to racial groups.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Babouvists planned insurrection and revolutionary war while Winstanley and Cabet were pacific, so the strands split.

free-public-college.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals demands common education for all and Winstanley's commonwealth provided schooling without charge.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Babouvists wanted to overthrow the Directory by insurrection, but Cabet and Winstanley sought peaceful change or model communities, so only a mild lean.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Most writers drew up a fixed blueprint of common ownership, as in Cabet's Icaria and the Equals' decrees, though Cabet and Winstanley favoured founding experimental communities.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals argues that all share the same faculties and needs, which grounds their claim to equal rights and goods.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals rejects merely legal equality and demands real equality, so fair elections alone would not make a government legitimate to them.

women-suffrage.rationale: Cabet advocated women's emancipation and the Manifesto speaks of differences only of age and sex, but the sources do not show women voting or holding office, so it is split.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals and Winstanley held that private property is the root of inequality and that land should be common, which rejects first-claim ownership.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet drew on Christian morals while Babouvists were secular, so strands split on scripture.

indirect-election.rationale: Babouvists and Cabet differed on political forms and the sources do not give one majority view.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The thinkers appealed to nature and to the common good, but not a spiritual bond to ancestral homeland; Babouvist internationalism and Christian strands split on it.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Babeuf's Equals and Cabet's Icarians based their politics on equal rights and justice, and Winstanley was pacific, so killing suspects without trial was foreign to them.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals declares the earth belongs to no one and its fruits to all, and Winstanley's Diggers claimed the common land for all.

self-ownership.rationale: The community of goods subordinated the individual to the commune, yet they also asserted equal natural rights over one's own labour, so strands differ.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Their attack on private property targeted the privileges of the rich and propertied, and the Manifesto denounces the inequality of rank and wealth.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Winstanley and Cabet argued from Christianity while Babouvists were secular, so no consistent view on denominational politics.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The Equals held that a just distribution means equality of goods, and rejected any claim of just inequality through property acquisition.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Labour as the source of wealth was a theme in Morelly, Babeuf and Cabet, though not formalised as a theory of value.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: The community of goods and the abolition of money and private property excluded a market economy, and no communist party existed.

police-more-powers.rationale: Winstanley kept officers to enforce laws but sought a peaceful commonwealth with no kings and no standing coercive state; more power for police and army is not a goal. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The Equals denounced a system where most toil for a tiny minority and demanded a common provision of needs, so cutting support for the poor opposes their core aims. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Inheritance of property should be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: The Equals' draft decree abolished inheritance and intestacy, passing goods to the national community at death.

missingStatements.text: All citizens should receive the same education and the same basic standard of living.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto of the Equals proposes one education and one standard of food for everyone, since all share the same faculties and needs.

notes: The strands diverge on religion (Winstanley and Cabet Christian, Babeuf and Morelly secular), on method (insurrection versus colonies), and on the family. Answers on those points are marked low or neutral.
